Who craves excess of days,
Scorning the common span
Of life, I judge that man
A giddy wight who walks in folly’s ways.
For the long years heap up a grievous load,
Scant pleasures, heavier pains,
Till not one joy remains
For him who lingers on life’s weary road
And come it slow or fast,
One doom of fate
Doth all await,
For dance and marriage bell,
The dirge and funeral knell.
Death the deliverer freeth all at last.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Not to be born at all / Is best, far best that can befall, / Next best, when born, with least delay / To trace the backward way” slowly and put it in my own words: The chorus ranks two fates: never to be born is best, and the next best, once born, is to go back the way you came, with as little delay as possible. Next, craft. I notice the wording itself ranks and rushes: “far best” lifts the first claim, “Next best” and “least delay” hurry a life already begun toward “the backward way.” The strongest word is “backward”: “the backward way” turns dying into a retracing of birth, a path walked quickly, in the voice of old men singing about long life and pain. Then, effect. What do lines 1284–1287 reveal about "Not to be born"? My answer: These four lines reveal the claim that it is best not to be born, and they belong to the elders’ grief. The scene just before, in which the daughters were restored, already stands beside this song as a picture of love and care.

followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Buffeted on every side.

items.text: What does the ode say happens to youth, before the later troubles are listed?
items.lookFor: Youth passes
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Youth passes.

items.text: Why compare Oedipus to a headland rather than a ship?
items.lookFor: A headland stays where it is while storms break on it from every side: the image grants his suffering and also his endurance, as a ship’s wreck would not.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: A ship can be wrecked and sink; a headland stays where it is. The elders picture their guest “as some headland on an iron-bound shore, / Lashed by the wintry blasts and surge’s roar” (lines 1300–1301). The image grants that he is “buffeted on every side” (line 1302), but it also makes him something the storms cannot carry away. The comparison holds both his suffering and his endurance.

items.text: What does “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” suggest about "Not to be born"? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: The most famous expression of despair in Greek tragedy, spoken as old men’s grief and already set beside a scene of love: the ode voices that grief while the scene before it showed love that makes life worth living.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode suggests how old age and long suffering can make life itself look like a burden: “Not to be born at all / Is best” (lines 1284–1285). Just before the ode, Oedipus held his daughters and said, “Death were not wholly bitter with you near” (line 1170). The ode is one voice of sorrow inside a play that keeps showing care and companionship.

items.text: Find one example of theme in “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”. What does it reveal about "Not to be born" that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A theme example, such as the loneliness of old age (“companionless”), explained for what it reveals: the elders’ despair is about loneliness as much as length of life, which the daughters’ presence answers.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode’s worst stage of life is “unregarded age, / Joyless, companionless and slow” (lines 1295–1296). The word “companionless” shows that the elders fear being alone and unregarded, not simply growing old. A plain statement that life is hard would miss this, and the scene just before it answers the fear: Oedipus is old and blind but not companionless.

items.text: How does the imagery in “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” shape what we understand about "Not to be born"?
items.lookFor: The imagery of a road, a load and storms from every direction, which makes long life a weight and a battering, and the headland image that turns the battering into endurance.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The images make long life a weight and a battering: “the long years heap up a grievous load” (line 1274), and storms come “Some from the sunset, some from orient morn” (line 1305). They shape our sense of Oedipus as a man struck from every side. The headland image at the end adds endurance: what is battered from every side still stands.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Who craves excess of…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from the opening (lines 1270–1277) with their connotations, such as “craves,” “excess,” “giddy wight” or “weary road,” showing the elders judging the wish for long life as folly.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The word “craves” (line 1270) makes the wish for long life sound like hunger or greed, and “giddy wight” (line 1273) calls such a person a dizzy fool. Together they judge the desire for more years as foolish appetite. The elders speak as old men disillusioned with what age brings.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is from general truths about life to “our guest,” and its effect is to tie the ode’s grief to Oedipus as he faces the hearing he dreads.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode turns at “Such ills not I alone, / He too our guest hath known” (lines 1298–1299). Before this the elders speak of everyone’s life; after it they speak of Oedipus. The effect is to bring the sorrow back to the man on stage just before he must face the son he called “hateful” (line 1232), so the audience expects pain rather than comfort.

items.text: How does “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” build on “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal link: Episode 3 ends with Oedipus reluctantly agreeing to hear his son, so the elders, waiting, reflect on the troubles that pile up in a long life.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Episode 3 ends with Oedipus yielding only grudgingly, “Grievous to me, my child, the boon ye win / By pleading” (lines 1263–1264). The ode reflects that grief: “Troubles on troubles follow, toils on toils” (line 1289). One more trouble is coming to an old man who already has many, and that makes the elders think about the burdens of a long life.

items.text: In “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about "Not to be born", as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive inferred from the ode: the elders speak in general truths, but the line “Such ills not I alone” shows they are describing their own old age as well as the guest’s.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode sounds like a general rule about life, but “Such ills not I alone, / He too our guest hath known” (lines 1298–1299) admits that the elders are also speaking of themselves. Their motive is personal: old men expressing their own weariness and finding in their guest a companion in suffering. That makes the ode sympathy, not cold philosophy.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (How does the scene in which the daughters were restored already sit beside this ode?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer to the bell-ringer (how the scene in which the daughters were restored already sits beside this ode), using the daughters’ care or the headland’s endurance as the counter-evidence.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: I first said the earlier scene does not sit beside this song. Now I see that it does: Oedipus said, “Death were not wholly bitter with you near” (line 1170), because his daughters were with him. The ode’s worst fear is age “Joyless, companionless and slow” (line 1296), and Oedipus is not companionless. The earlier scene answers the ode with love rather than argument.

items.text: Where does tone / mood appear in “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”, and how does it connect "Not to be born" to the larger concern with curse and mercy?
items.lookFor: Where the tone shifts from bitter judgment to pity for the guest, and how that connects to curse and mercy: the ode feels for a man buffeted on every side just before he is asked to show mercy to his son.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The tone moves from bitter judgment (“A giddy wight who walks in folly’s ways,” line 1273) to pity for the guest, “So is he buffeted on every side” (line 1302). That pity matters for curse and mercy. The elders show mercy to Oedipus just before he is asked to show it to his son, which leaves the audience asking whether a man so battered can give what the elders give him.

items.text: Open question: does the play agree with this ode? Defend any position with evidence.
items.lookFor: A defended position: the play does not simply agree; it frames the ode as old men’s grief and answers it with care, endurance and the gods’ concern. A counterpoint notes how much suffering the play does show.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the play understands the ode but does not simply rest in it, even in this section. The ode says “Death the deliverer freeth all at last” (line 1283), but the same day’s evidence gives Oedipus his daughters’ love, “I have my darlings” (line 1169), and the elders themselves picture him as a headland that endures (line 1300). Counter-line: the play does show suffering on every side (lines 1302–1307), so the ode’s sorrow is earned, even if it is not the only word this section gives us.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The most famous expression of despair in Greek tragedy, set beside a scene of love that came just before it. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines, qualifying the claim by pointing out that at this point the play’s counterweight is the love shown in the scene before the ode, not an ending we have not yet read.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. The despair is strong: “Not to be born at all / Is best” (lines 1284–1285). But the frame is already there: the ode ends by comparing Oedipus to a headland that stands against the storm (lines 1300–1302), and the scene before it showed love (line 1170). The counterweight at this point is that earlier scene and the headland, not a later act we have not yet read.

items.text: No character acts in “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”; the elders reflect. Which attitude toward a long life does the ode present as wisest, and which as least wise? Judge them by a standard you name, and say whether you accept it.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two attitudes the ode describes, for example the man who craves endless years against acceptance of the common span, with lines and a counter-view from the daughters’ care.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the ode’s own standard, accepting the ordinary span of life, the man who “craves excess of days, / Scorning the common span” (lines 1270–1271) is least wise, and the wise attitude is acceptance that “One doom of fate / Doth all await” (lines 1279–1280). A student could challenge the standard: Oedipus’s wish to live near his daughters (line 1170) seems wiser than the ode’s weariness.

items.text: You are directing “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of "Not to be born".
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the chorus turning toward Oedipus at “He too our guest hath known” or sound effects of wind and sea for the headland, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) Sing the opening lines (lines 1270–1297) facing the audience, as general reflection, then have the elders turn toward Oedipus at “He too our guest hath known” (line 1299), so the sorrow lands on him. (2) Under the headland image (lines 1300–1307), bring in the sound of wind and surf from different sides while Oedipus sits upright and still. The audience sees him battered but standing.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1270–1307: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: To what does the ode compare Oedipus? (A headland on a storm-beaten shore, lines 1300–1302.) Why/how: Why does the ode call the worst stage “unregarded age” (line 1295)? (Being old and ignored is worse than being old.) Should/what if: Should the elders have sung this ode in front of their suffering guest? (Answers weigh honesty and sympathy against comfort.)

items.text: Connect “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”, with its focus on "Not to be born", to law against force: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about law against force, the question’s theme. The link is weak here; the ode names “Envy, sedition, strife” and war as life’s troubles but proposes no law. A strong answer says what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is weak in this ode. It lists “Envy, sedition, strife, / Carnage and war” (lines 1292–1293) as the stuff of life but offers no law against them, only endurance. The theme is waiting: Oedipus has agreed to hear a son who came as a suppliant under the god’s protection. To strengthen the link, Sophocles must show whether custom and law can govern that hearing, or whether strife wins again.

items.text: Is the theme in “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” effective in presenting "Not to be born", or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion (honest grief or heavy pessimism?), with a line that meets the criterion and one that might miss it, mindful that this is grief and age speaking in a song.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because the grief is concrete and tied to a person, ending with the headland (lines 1300–1307), not an abstract sermon. Counter-line: the run “Pain, pain for ever pain” (line 1290) and the piled-up list of troubles may feel heavy-handed to a modern reader. A fair review notes that the ode is grief and old age speaking, and the play sets other voices against it.

items.text: Compare how “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” treats "Not to be born" with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (another text about the burdens of old age or a lament) and one thing the ode sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare Dylan Thomas’s villanelle that urges his dying father to fight against death. The ode sees a different side of age: weariness and loneliness, “Joyless, companionless and slow” (line 1296). It sees that what makes old age hardest is being “unregarded” (line 1295). That is why the daughters’ care in the play matters so much.

items.text: Predict what “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, the ode’s list of “sedition, strife” and war and Oedipus’s grudging promise to hear his son, about the meeting with the son, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: the ode names “Envy, sedition, strife, / Carnage and war” (lines 1292–1293) as the tale of life. Clue 2: Oedipus agreed to hear his son only grudgingly, calling him “my hateful son” (line 1232). A reasonable prediction is that the son will come asking for something tied to strife, and that his father will not receive him kindly. After reading, students check how far the ode’s dark mood prepared for the scene.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about "Not to be born"?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: old people reflect bitterly on the burdens of long life, then turn their pity on a friend who has suffered more. It names two details that must stay, framing it as grief.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In a care-home lounge, residents talk bitterly about how long life has brought more losses than joys, then one nods toward a blind newcomer and says he has had it worse than any of them, though he is still standing. Two things must stay: the turn from the elders’ own sorrow to the guest, “He too our guest hath known” (line 1299), and the image of endurance at the end (lines 1300–1302), so it reads as grief and sympathy.
